newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South African manufacturing confidence rises.
newsitem.headline: South African manufacturing confidence rises.

text.p: General business conditions and confidence in the manufacturing sector improved further in the first quarter of this year, confounding bearish expectations, the University of Stellenbosch's Bureau for Economic Research said on Thursday.

But it warned that high consumer debt, high real interest rates, higher prices, inventory disinvestment and the strengthening of the rand could place a damper on otherwise optimistic expectations for the months ahead.
BER said that the sharp growth in agricultural output last year had concealed the slowdown in growth in the non-agricultural sector to two percent from four percent in 1995.
"The slowdown in manufacturing volume growth from 7.5 percent to 0.5 percent over the corresponding period was quite sharp," it said.

On the demand side, real growth in gross domestic expenditure fell by two percent in the last two quarters of 1996. But manufacturing volumes improved, mainly because of increased exports, boosting confidence in the sector.
BER said its latest manufacturing survey had found that general business conditions had "improved noticeably" in the first quarter.
"Somewhat bearish expectations were confounded, particularly regarding the domestic market," BER said.

"Significant growth in domestic sales, production and order volumes materialised, both compared to the fourth quarter of 1996 and the situation a year ago. Manufacturers were significantly more optimistic regarding general business conditions in the 1 months ahead."
There was real growth in export sales and orders in most sub-sectors as the drive to improve production capacity appeared to have received fresh stimulus.
Improved domestic demand was also encouraging but it was not entirely certain whether this would be maintained in the second quarter.

"While the general improvement could still prove to be hesitant at first, the BER is optimistic that the manufacturing sector could experience a renewed growth phase within the following 12 months," it said.
Manufacturers were likely to experience increased demand from abroad because of improving world economic prospects and a more competitive positions following the sharp depreciation of the rand.
As a percentage of total merchandise exports, manufactured exports increased to 29.5 percent in 1996 compared to 15.7 percent in 1995.

BER said that export markets were well diversified, exporters were successfully developing niche markets in industrialised countries and that exporters to Africa appeared to have a comparative advantage.
"Manufacturers are therefore well positioned to exploit opportunities in the export recovery currently taking shape," BER said.

After the wave of fixed investment in the manufacturing sector in 1994, 1995 and part of 1996 to modernise plant and equipment, BER said it hoped that the next round of fixed investment would be aimed at expanding production capacity and employment.
